title: Make or Do?
intro: Make a mistake, do your homework, make progress, do business — match each phrase to the verb it actually takes.

A2.why: Household chores usually take “do”: do the dishes, do the cleaning.

A2.right: make (make a mistake = get something wrong)
A2.why: Spanish says “cometer un error”; English always says make a mistake, never “do”.
Tasks and jobs take “do”: do your homework, do the ironing.
“Make” is for creating something new: make a cake, make a paella.

A2.right: do (do someone a favour = help them)
A2.why: Fixed phrase: “Could you do me a favour?” = please help me.
Sounds you produce take “make”: make a noise, make a sound.
Chores take “do”: do the shopping, do the cooking.
English says make a decision (or “take” in British English), never “do a decision”.

A2.right: make (make the bed = tidy the sheets)
A2.why: Spanish “hacer la cama”, and English agrees: make the bed.

A2.right: do (do the ironing = press the clothes)
A2.why: Another household chore, so “do”: do the ironing, do the washing.

A2.right: make (make a cup of tea = prepare a drink)
A2.why: Preparing food and drink takes “make”: make a coffee, make lunch.

A2.right: do (do the cleaning = clean the house)
A2.why: Chores ending in -ing usually take “do”: do the cleaning, do the shopping.

B1.why: Spanish “hacer progresos” becomes make progress, never “do progress”.
Spanish “hacer un esfuerzo” becomes make an effort.
You do business with a company: buy, sell and make deals.

B1.right: do (do your best = try as hard as you can)
B1.why: Fixed phrase: do your best. “Make your best” is a common mistake.
You make a call; “do a call” is wrong.
Activities of investigation take “do”: do research, never “make research”.
Spanish says “ganar dinero”, but English says make money.
Activities take “do”: do exercise, do yoga. Not “make exercise”.

B1.right: make (make a complaint = say formally you are unhappy)
B1.why: Things you say take “make”: make a complaint, make a suggestion.

B1.right: do (do a course = study a subject)
B1.why: Spanish “hacer un curso” works the same in English: do an English course.
Like Spanish “hacer amigos”: make friends, never “do friends”.

B1.right: do (do the paperwork = deal with the forms)
B1.why: Office tasks take “do”: do the paperwork, do the accounts.

B2.right: make (make a difference = have an effect)
B2.why: Spanish “marcar la diferencia” becomes make a difference.

B2.right: do (do damage = break or spoil something)
B2.why: Do damage = cause damage; “make damage” is a typical Spanish-speaker mistake.

B2.right: make (make an appointment = arrange a meeting)
B2.why: You make an appointment with the doctor: you arrange it. Spanish “pedir cita”.

B2.right: do (do a good job = perform well)
B2.why: Work you perform takes “do”: do a good job, do a job well.

B2.right: make (make a profit = earn more than you spend)
B2.why: Like make money: make a profit, make a loss.
Same pattern as damage: do harm, never “make harm”. “It does no harm to ask.”

B2.right: make (make an impression = affect how people see you)
B2.why: You make an impression on someone: you change how they see you.

B2.right: do (do the washing up = clean the dishes)
B2.why: British English for washing the dishes after a meal: do the washing up.

B2.right: make (make an excuse = give a reason to avoid something)
B2.why: Things you say take “make”: he made an excuse not to come.

B2.right: do (do someone good = be good for their health)
B2.why: A week by the sea in Dénia will do you good.
Plans you organise take “make”: make arrangements, make plans.
Work on your appearance takes “do”: do your hair, do your make-up.

C1.why: Always plural: make amends = do something to repair a wrong.

C1.right: do (do justice to something = represent it fairly)
C1.why: “The photo doesn't do justice to the Albufera” = the real place is more beautiful.
Like make progress, but slowly and against difficulty: we're making headway.

C1.right: do (do the honours = perform a ceremonial task)
C1.why: Said when someone pours the drinks or cuts the cake: “Will you do the honours?”

C1.right: make (make a fortune = become very rich)
C1.why: Like make money, but much more: some prospectors made a fortune in the gold rush.

C1.right: do (do one's duty = fulfil an obligation)
C1.why: Obligations take “do”: the sheriff did his duty and arrested his own brother.

C1.right: make (make a scene = cause a public fuss)
C1.why: Make a scene = shout or cry in public; Spanish “montar un número”.

C1.right: do (do wonders for something = have a great positive effect)
C1.why: “Do wonders for” = have a very good effect: sea air does wonders for your health.

C1.right: make (make a killing = earn a lot of money quickly)
C1.why: Informal and nothing violent: “He made a killing on the property market.”

C1.right: do (do time = serve a prison sentence)
C1.why: Informal: the outlaw did time in Yuma prison before going straight.

C1.right: make (make a beeline for = go straight towards)
C1.why: Like a bee flying straight home: at parties he makes a beeline for the food.
If there's no sugar, we'll do without: we'll manage without it.
